title: A nice little boost without caffeine
content: I've been using the Neutonic Nootropic Focus Blend Powder (Peach Mango & Wild Berry) for a few weeks now, and overall, I'm pretty impressed. As someone who's sensitive to caffeine but still needs a mental edge, this caffeine-free option has been a godsend.  Pros:  The most noticeable benefit for me is the sustained mental clarity. I feel like my thoughts are sharper, and I'm less prone to that mid-afternoon brain fog. There's a subtle but definite boost in focus, especially when I'm tackling tasks that require sustained concentration. I also appreciate that it's zero sugar, so no energy crashes later on. The Wild Berry flavor is okay, but not as enjoyable as the Peach Mango for my taste. Also, at roughly a dollar a stick, it's not the cheapest daily supplement, so it's something to factor into your budget if you plan on using it consistently.  Overall:  If you're looking for a caffeine-free way to support your cognitive function, memory, and focus without the jitters or sugar crash, Neutonic is definitely worth a try. It delivers a reliable, gentle lift that helps me stay on top of my game.

Taking into consideration the stack of caffeine, nootropics and vitamins in the ingredients, I’m not surprised that the Neutonic drinks can provide some marginal gains when it comes to focus and concentration. Overall, I’d say that I’ve experienced some enhancement to cognitive function that’s free from jitters or an uncomfortable buzz.But what does it taste like? This is where I’m a bit less enamoured unfortunately. I thought of old school Lilt on first try but eventually it was Myprotein Clear Whey that sprang to mind. The sweeteners used are the same in both products and it’s this prominent and lingering aftertaste that stays with me so I find Neutonic functionally enjoyable as opposed to unique and/or delicious. My preference is for natural sugars or syrups in health and energy drinks and the use of artificial sweeteners, even stevia, has ruined a few old favourite brands for me…Personal taste aside, congratulations to everyone behind Neutonic and all the best with development and rolling it out worldwide. I’ll keep an eye out for it locally and will give the other flavours a whirl when available.

But I’ve been drinking the orange flavour for 4 of the last 5 days and I have genuinely seen a noticeable improvement in the output in my laptop work.I run my own marketing business and I’m ADHD AF, so I’m great focussing on my creative work, but terrible when I’m doing (important) admin/laptop work. After drinking a can in the mornings this week I’ve found myself getting 30-40 minutes of really focussed laptop work done several times throughout the day - and that’s HUGE for me!You don’t ‘feel’ anything (obviously) and tbh I’ve kinda forgotten that I’ve drank it after an hour or so. Then I’ve suddenly found myself in a really awesome flow state and managed to keep going.I bashed out two proposals in a day this week! content: This product did exactly what I needed: it helped my nicotine cravings dissipate. Expect an adjustment period, though. The first tin is essentially a wash. Overall, it’s a strong pouch built on a great concept, with plenty of room to refine, and I’m curious to see how it evolves. It served its purpose, and I’d buy it again. title: Very effective for my brain fog, focus, and executive function.
content: I'm actually not surprised at all that this Neutonic Nootropic Brain Supplement is effective for me; I already know from prior experience that Citicoline and Rhodiola rosea are two of the most effective cognitive supplements for me personally, out of all the myriad supplements I've tried for my severe ADHD. The dosage is also in line with my personal sweet spot; if I am only supplementing Rhodiola, I might need a higher dosage (500-700mg), but I've noticed that when it is supported by certain other nootropics that are present in this blend, I can get away with 400mg.    While I personally don't find Ginseng, Bacopa and Gingko Biloba stand-outs on their own (at least not in the way where it's super noticeable like with Rhodiola and Citicoline), I have noticed that they seem to have an important supportive role for me and seem to make the entire blend a bit more effective versus simply taking Rhodiola alone, for example.    This supplement also contains an array of B-vitamins, as deficiency in any B-vitamins is known to cause fatigue. This is why you see so many of these cognitive complexes include them; it's practical to try and fill in a relatively common nutrition gap.    I've never tried this brand before, but I am familiar enough with the impacts of these ingredients to say that I believe this is a legitimate supplement and includes its advertised ingredients. I take this when I first wake up, along with an electrolyte drink, and I find it helps me get my brain running and smooths out the executive function a bit for the rest of my day. To give a precise breakdown, I take it when my alarm goes off at 4PM (I am a third shifter), and I start feeling it wear off typically around 2-3AM.    If you are also interested in this for ADHD support, be advised it mostly seems to benefit executive function, focus/brain fog, and time blindness for me. I don't think it helps with emotional dysregulation at all, for me at least. With that said, of course, be mindful that what works for one person may not work for someone else. I can only report on my own direct experience.    It's a bit pricy compared to some other similar complexes, but if you are like me and live somewhere that experiences frequent ADHD medication shortages, I do think this is worthwhile to help keep yourself functional even during those times where access is interrupted or limited, or as general support for your medication regimen. As always, confer with your doctor to ensure that nothing in this complex may interfere with any health conditions or medications you may take!    Also, finally, be aware that it is advised to take a week or so off from Rhodiola every few months. There is some conflicting evidence and some people believe this recommendation may be an old wives' tale, but until we have more concrete research disputing the advisement to take breaks to keep up efficacy, I think it is smarter to err on the side of caution and take those breaks for now.
